steps.why: Three sp² hybrid orbitals point to the corners of an equilateral triangle in one plane. With three bond pairs and no lone pair on boron, the molecule keeps that flat triangular shape and 120° angles.
common_mistakes: Writing that fluorine bonds through its 3p orbitals. The valence orbitals of fluorine are 2s and 2p.
Calling BF₃ pyramidal. Boron carries no lone pair here, so the three bonds stay in one plane.
steps.memory_tip: Three bonds and no lone pair on boron: sp², flat, 120°.
steps.margin_note: Give the shape and the bond angle together; the word sp² alone does not describe a shape.

steps.label: BH₄⁻ is sp³ and tetrahedral
lines: In BH₄⁻ boron uses four sp³ hybrid
orbitals and forms four B–H bonds.
Three of them are normal covalent bonds.
The fourth is a coordinate bond, made
when a hydride ion H⁻ donates its lone
pair, and that pair brings the negative
Once the ion has formed, all four B–H
bonds are the same length and strength.
The ion is tetrahedral with H–B–H bond
steps.why: BH₃ is a boron atom joined to three hydrogens, and it still has one empty orbital. A hydride ion H⁻ adds its lone pair to that empty orbital, so boron gains a fourth pair. The hybridisation changes from sp² to sp³ and the four pairs move to the corners of a tetrahedron.
common_mistakes: Giving the shape as square planar. Four bond pairs and no lone pair make a tetrahedron.
Keeping boron as sp² in BH₄⁻. The fourth bond makes it sp³.
steps.memory_tip: Four bonds around boron: sp³, tetrahedral, 109°28′.
steps.margin_note: Write the angle 109°28′ beside the word tetrahedral.

insider_note: The question asks two things about each species, the shape and the hybridisation, so four short statements complete the whole answer.
